rows.stem: The charge required for the reduction of 1 mol of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) is
rows.solution:
Work from the change in oxidation state, not from formula masses. In \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) manganese is \(+7\); in \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) it is \(+4\). Each manganese therefore gains THREE electrons:
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 3e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
One mole of permanganate needs three moles of electrons, so the charge required is 3 F. The distractor 5 F is the answer for reduction to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is what happens in strongly acidic solution.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Which among the following is a false statement ?

options.label: A
options.text: Rate of zero order reaction is independent of initial concentration of reactant.

options.label: B
options.text: Half-life of a zero order reaction is inversely proportional to the rate constant.

options.label: C
options.text: Molecularity of a reaction may be zero.

rows.solution:
Three of the statements are true. A zero order rate is \(k\) and so does not depend on the initial concentration. A zero order half-life is \(t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{R}]_0/2k\), which is indeed inversely proportional to \(k\). And \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\) is the first order result.

The false statement is that molecularity may be zero. Molecularity counts the molecules that must collide in an elementary step, so it is a whole number and at least 1 — it can be neither zero nor fractional. ORDER can be zero or fractional, and confusing the two is exactly what this question tests.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The number of molecules that react with each other in an elementary reaction is a measure of the :
rows.solution:
The number of molecules, atoms or ions that must collide simultaneously for an elementary reaction to take place is its MOLECULARITY. It is a theoretical quantity, read off the mechanism, and is necessarily a small whole number.

Order, by contrast, is obtained from the experimentally measured rate law; activation energy is the energy barrier the colliding molecules must clear; and stoichiometry describes the proportions in the balanced equation, which for a complex reaction has nothing to do with how many molecules collide in any one step.

rows.subtopic: Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements
rows.stem: The element having \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{1}}\) electronic configuration is
rows.solution:
Copper has 24 core plus outer electrons totalling 29, and its ground state configuration is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1\) rather than the expected \(3d^9 4s^2\), because a completely filled d subshell is the more stable arrangement.

Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\), chromium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\) — the other exception, for a half-filled subshell — and manganese is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\).

rows.stem: The complex ions \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}}\) are called
rows.solution:
The two ions have the same formula and the same ligands; what differs is WHICH ATOM of the nitrite ligand is attached to the cobalt. In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\) the bond is through nitrogen (nitrito-N); in \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]^{2+}}\) it is through oxygen (nitrito-O). Isomers differing only in the donor atom used by an AMBIDENTATE ligand are called linkage isomers.

Ionisation isomers differ in which ion is inside the sphere and which is the counter ion; coordination isomers exchange ligands between two metal centres; geometrical isomers differ in the spatial arrangement of the same bonds.

rows.stem:
The diamagnetic species is :
[At. No. Co = 27, Fe = 26, Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
A species is diamagnetic only when every electron is paired.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\) nickel is \(+2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\); cyanide is a strong field ligand and pairs those eight electrons into four orbitals, giving a square planar \(dsp^2\) complex with NO unpaired electron — diamagnetic.

In \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) the weak field chloride leaves two unpaired. In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) iron is \(3d^5\) and, even with pairing, one electron is left over. In \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) cobalt is \(3d^6\) with the weak field fluoride, leaving four unpaired. All three of those are paramagnetic.

rows.stem: Which is the correct IUPAC name for
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED - the compound exists ONLY as a drawn structure: a benzene ring with a CH3 group bonded at the top vertex and a Cl at the para (bottom) vertex. The stem names no compound at all without it. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The compound is a benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a chlorine atom at the para position. Both substituents are named as prefixes on the parent benzene, cited alphabetically — chloro before methyl — and numbered to give the lowest locants, so the chlorine is at position 1 and the methyl at position 4.

The IUPAC name is 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene. Reversing the two prefixes breaks the alphabetical rule; "methylchlorobenzene" gives no locants at all; and toluene is the common name for the compound without the chlorine.

rows.stem: What will be formed after oxidation reaction of secondary alcohol with chromic anhydride \(\mathrm{(CrO_3)}\) ?
rows.solution:
Chromic anhydride is a mild, non-aqueous oxidising agent, and the outcome depends on the class of alcohol. A SECONDARY alcohol has one hydrogen on the carbon bearing the \(-\mathrm{OH}\); removing that hydrogen together with the hydroxyl hydrogen creates a \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) group flanked by two carbon substituents — a KETONE.
\(\mathrm{R_2CH-OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}} \mathrm{R_2C{=}O}\)
A primary alcohol would give an aldehyde under the same conditions, and a tertiary alcohol, having no hydrogen on that carbon, resists oxidation altogether. A ketone cannot be oxidised further without breaking a carbon-carbon bond, which is why the reaction stops cleanly here.

rows.stem: The conversion of phenol to salicylic acid can be accomplished by
rows.solution:
Kolbe's reaction converts phenol into salicylic acid. Phenol is first treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium phenoxide, which is a stronger nucleophile than phenol itself; carbon dioxide then attacks the ring ortho to the oxygen, and acidification gives 2-hydroxybenzoic acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{CO_2}} \text{salicylic acid}\)
Reimer-Tiemann gives salicylALDEHYDE, not the acid; Friedel-Crafts introduces alkyl or acyl groups; and coupling is a diazonium reaction.

rows.stem: Which of the following is/are examples of denaturation of protein ?
rows.solution:
Denaturation is the loss of a protein's native three-dimensional structure, and with it its biological activity, when heat or a change in pH disturbs the weak interactions holding the chain folded. Coagulating the white of an egg by heating is the standard example, and curdling milk — where acid unfolds the casein — is another. So both (A) and (B) are examples.

Clotting of blood is not denaturation: it is a controlled enzymatic cascade converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, with the proteins involved keeping their structures and functions throughout.

rows.stem: Nucleotides are joined together by
rows.solution:
Within a nucleic acid the sugar of one nucleotide is joined to the sugar of the next through a phosphate group, which esterifies an \(-\mathrm{OH}\) on each — one ester bond on either side of the same phosphorus. That double ester is called a PHOSPHODIESTER linkage, and the repeating sugar-phosphate chain it builds is the backbone of DNA and RNA.

A glycosidic linkage joins sugar units in a carbohydrate, a peptide linkage joins amino acids in a protein, and hydrogen bonds hold the two DNA strands together but do not join nucleotides along a strand.

rows.stem: Scurvy is caused due to deficiency of
rows.solution:
Scurvy is caused by deficiency of vitamin C, whose chemical name is ascorbic acid. Its symptoms are bleeding gums and poor wound healing, because vitamin C is needed to make collagen.

Deficiency of vitamin \(\mathrm{B_1}\), thiamine, causes beri-beri, and of vitamin \(\mathrm{B_2}\), riboflavin, cheilosis and digestive disorders. Glutamic acid is an amino acid, not a vitamin.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : In a first order reaction, if the concentration of the reactant is doubled, its half-life is also doubled.
Reason (R) : The half-life of a reaction does not depend upon the initial concentration of the reactant in a first order reaction.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
For a first order reaction the half-life is
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)
which contains no concentration term at all. Doubling the initial concentration therefore leaves the half-life unchanged, so the Assertion, which says it doubles, is FALSE.

The Reason states exactly that independence and is TRUE — indeed it is the fact that makes the Assertion false. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Cu cannot liberate \(\mathrm{H_2}\) on reaction with dilute mineral acids.
Reason (R) : Cu has positive electrode potential.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute mineral acids, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason gives the cause. A metal displaces hydrogen from an acid only if it is the stronger reducing agent, that is if its electrode potential is negative. Copper's \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}\) is \(+0.34\) V, the only positive value in the first transition series, so copper is not oxidised by \(\mathrm{H^+}\) and no hydrogen is evolved. It dissolves only in oxidising acids such as nitric acid, where a different reduction supplies the driving force. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel Phthalimide synthesis.
Reason (R) : Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution reaction with the anion formed by phthalimide.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason names the exact cause. The synthesis depends on the phthalimide anion displacing a halide by nucleophilic substitution; an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution, because its \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring and the electron-rich ring repels the incoming nucleophile. Without that first step the method cannot even begin. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Vitamin D cannot be stored in our body.
Reason (R) : Vitamin D is fat soluble vitamin and is not excreted from the body in urine.
rows.context: For question number 13 to 16, two statements are given - one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Vitamin D CAN be stored in the body, so the Assertion is false. The Reason explains why: vitamin D is fat soluble, and fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue rather than being excreted in the urine. So the Reason is true and it is precisely the ground on which the Assertion fails.

This is also why an excess of vitamin D can be harmful, whereas an excess of a water-soluble vitamin such as C is simply excreted.

rows.stem: The rate constant for a zero order reaction \(\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\) is 0.0030 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}s^{-1}}\). How long will it take for the initial concentration of A to fall from 0.10 M to 0.075 M ?
rows.solution:
For a zero order reaction the rate is constant, so the concentration falls linearly with time:
\([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt \implies k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0 - [\mathrm{R}]}{t}\)

Rearranging for the time and substituting,
\(t = \dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0 - [\mathrm{R}]}{k} = \dfrac{0.10 - 0.075}{0.0030} = \dfrac{0.025}{0.0030}\)
\(t = 8.33\ \mathrm{s}\)

No logarithm is needed, which is the signature of zero order.

rows.stem: The decomposition of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) on platinum surface is zero order reaction. What are the rates of production of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2}\) if k = \(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\) ?
rows.solution:
The decomposition is
\(2\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2}\)

and the single rate of reaction relates the three species through their coefficients:
\(-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{NH_3}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{N_2}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{H_2}]}{\Delta t} = k\)

Because the reaction is zero order, that rate is simply \(k\), independent of any concentration. So
\(\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{N_2}]}{\Delta t} = k = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)
\(\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{H_2}]}{\Delta t} = 3k = 7.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

Hydrogen is produced three times as fast as nitrogen, exactly as the stoichiometry requires.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Pseudo first order reaction
(b) Half-life period of reaction \(\mathrm{(t_{1/2})}\)
rows.solution:
(a) A pseudo first order reaction is one whose true molecularity is higher — usually bimolecular — but which behaves kinetically as first order because one reactant is present in such large excess that its concentration hardly changes and can be absorbed into the rate constant. Acid hydrolysis of an ester in dilute aqueous solution is the standard example, water being the reactant in excess.

(b) The half-life period of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of a reactant falls to one half of its initial value — equivalently, the time in which half the reaction is complete. For a first order reaction it is \(0.693/k\) and does not depend on the starting concentration; for other orders it does.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Examine the following observations :
(a) Transition elements generally form coloured compounds.
(b) Zinc is not regarded as a transition element.
rows.solution:
(a) Because their ions have partly filled d subshells. The ligands or surrounding ions split the five d orbitals into sets of different energy, and an electron can absorb a photon of visible light to jump from a lower set to a higher one. The colour seen is the complement of the light absorbed in this d-d transition. An ion with an empty or a completely filled d subshell has no such transition available and its compounds are colourless.

(b) A transition element is defined as one having a partially filled d subshell in its ground state or in one of its common oxidation states. Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^2\) and its only common ion, \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), is \(3d^{10}\). The d subshell is completely filled throughout, so zinc does not meet the definition — and correspondingly it forms colourless compounds, shows no variable valency and is a poor catalyst.

rows.stem:
Name the following coordination compounds according to IUPAC norms :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)Cl]Cl_2}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[CrCl_2\,(en)_2]\,Cl}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Two chloride ions outside contribute \(-2\), so the complex cation is \(+2\). Inside it the four ammine and one aqua ligand are neutral and the chlorido ligand is \(-1\), which puts cobalt at \(+3\). Ligands are cited alphabetically — ammine, aqua, chlorido:
tetraamineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride

(b) One chloride outside contributes \(-1\), so the cation is \(+1\); inside, two chlorido ligands at \(-1\) each and two neutral ethane-1,2-diamine ligands put chromium at \(+3\). Chlorido comes before ethane-1,2-diamine alphabetically, and the latter takes the prefix bis because its own name contains numerals:
dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)chromium(III) chloride

rows.stem:
(a) In the following pair of halogen compounds, which compound undergoes \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction faster and why ?
(b) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their reactivity towards \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) displacement :
2-Bromo-2-methylbutane, 1-Bromopentane, 2-Bromopentane.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED for sub-part (a) - the 'following pair' exists ONLY as two drawn skeletal structures joined by the word 'and': on the left a quaternary carbon carrying Cl upwards and three methyl bonds (2-chloro-2-methylpropane), on the right a five-carbon zig-zag chain carrying Cl on the middle carbon (3-chloropentane). Sub-part (a) names no compound in text. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) The tertiary halide reacts faster. An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction goes through a carbocation formed in the slow step, so the reaction is as fast as that cation is stable. A tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three alkyl groups releasing electron density towards the positive centre, and it is also planar and relatively unhindered once formed. The primary halide in the pair would have to form a primary carbocation, which is far too unstable, so it reacts by the bimolecular route instead and not by \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) at all.

(b) An \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction needs the nucleophile to reach the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, so the LESS crowded that carbon is, the faster the reaction — the exact reverse of the \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) order. 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is tertiary and most hindered, 2-bromopentane is secondary, and 1-bromopentane is primary and least hindered. The increasing order of reactivity is
2-bromo-2-methylbutane \(<\) 2-bromopentane \(<\) 1-bromopentane

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: At 25 °C the saturated vapour pressure of water is 24 mm Hg. Find the saturated vapour pressure of a 5% aqueous solution of urea at the same temperature. (Molar mass of urea = 60 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
A 5% aqueous solution contains 5 g of urea in 100 g of solution, so the water is \(100 - 5 = 95\) g. Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute, which for a dilute solution may be taken as \(n_2/n_1\):

\(\dfrac{p_1^{\circ} - p_1}{p_1^{\circ}} = \dfrac{w_2 \times M_1}{M_2 \times w_1}\)

\(\dfrac{24 - p_1}{24} = \dfrac{5 \times 18}{60 \times 95} = \dfrac{3}{190}\)

\(24 - p_1 = \dfrac{3 \times 24}{190} = 0.379\)

\(p_1 = 23.62\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

The commonest slip is taking the water as 100 g rather than 95 g; the 5% is by mass OF THE SOLUTION.

rows.stem: The electrical resistance of a column of 0.05 M NaOH solution of area 0.8 \(\mathrm{cm^2}\) and length 40 cm is \(5 \times 10^{3}\) ohm. Calculate its resistivity, conductivity and molar conductivity.
rows.solution:
Resistivity comes from the measured resistance and the cell's geometry:
\(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{3} \times 0.8}{40} = 100\ \Omega\ \mathrm{cm}\)

Conductivity is its reciprocal:
\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \dfrac{1}{100} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

and molar conductivity follows from the concentration:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{10^{-2} \times 1000}{0.05} = 2 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note that \(A\) and \(l\) enter resistivity the OTHER way round from how they enter resistance: a longer column has more resistance but the same resistivity.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete and balance the following chemical equations :
(a) \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + \mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{513\ K}]{\text{Heat}}\)
(c) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2S} + \mathrm{H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(a) Permanganate oxidises oxalate to carbon dioxide in acid and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O} + 10\mathrm{CO_2}\)

(b) Heating potassium permanganate decomposes it, the manganese disproportionating to the \(+6\) manganate and the \(+4\) dioxide while oxygen is evolved:
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{513\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

(c) Acidified dichromate oxidises hydrogen sulphide to free sulphur:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{H_2S} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{S} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Six electrons pass in each of the three: two chromiums taking three each, and three sulphides giving two each.

rows.stem:
Using valence bond theory, explain the hybridization and magnetic character of the following :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\)
[At. no. : Co = 27, Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\). Cobalt is \(+3\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Ammonia is a STRONG field ligand, so it forces all six electrons to pair into three of the \(3d\) orbitals, leaving two \(3d\) orbitals empty. Those two, with the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals, accept the six lone pairs from the six ammonia molecules.
Hybridisation: \(d^2sp^3\), an inner orbital octahedral complex.
Magnetic character: with every electron paired, DIAMAGNETIC.

(b) \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\). Nickel here is in the ZERO oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide is a strong field ligand and drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10} 4s^0\). The empty \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals then accept the four lone pairs from the four carbonyl groups.
Hybridisation: \(sp^3\), tetrahedral.
Magnetic character: with no unpaired electron, DIAMAGNETIC.

rows.stem:
(a) Define the following :
(i) Enantiomers
(ii) Racemic mixture
(b) Why is chlorobenzene resistant to nucleophilic substitution reaction ?
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Enantiomers are the two stereoisomers of a compound that are related to each other as non-superimposable mirror images. They have identical physical and chemical properties in an achiral environment and differ only in rotating plane-polarised light equally but in opposite directions.

(ii) A racemic mixture is an equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers of a compound, the \(d\) and \(l\) forms. Their rotations cancel exactly, so the mixture is optically inactive.

(b) Three reasons, all pulling the same way. The lone pair on chlorine is delocalised into the ring, so the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond acquires partial double bond character, becomes shorter and stronger, and is harder to break. The carbon carrying the chlorine is \(sp^2\) rather than \(sp^3\), and an \(sp^2\) carbon is more electronegative and holds the shared pair more tightly. And the electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud of the ring repels the approaching nucleophile. A phenyl cation, which a unimolecular route would require, is also highly unstable.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Explain the following reactions and write chemical equation involved :
(a) Wolff-Kishner reduction
(b) Etard reaction
(c) Cannizzaro reaction
rows.solution:
(a) Wolff-Kishner reduction. The carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone is reduced all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\). The compound is first condensed with hydrazine to give the hydrazone, and that is then heated with sodium or potassium hydroxide in a high-boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol; nitrogen is expelled and the hydrocarbon remains.
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{C{=}N-NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

(b) Etard reaction. Chromyl chloride oxidises the methyl group of toluene to a chromium complex, and hydrolysis of that complex gives benzaldehyde. The complex is what protects the product: without it the oxidation would carry on to benzoic acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{2. }\mathrm{H_3O^+},\ \Delta]{\text{1. }\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2},\ \mathrm{CS_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)

(c) Cannizzaro reaction. An aldehyde with NO \(\alpha\) hydrogen, heated with concentrated alkali, undergoes self-oxidation and reduction: one molecule is reduced to the alcohol and another oxidised to the salt of the acid.
\(2\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH\ (conc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}\)

rows.stem:
Write the structures of A, B and C in the following sequence of reactions :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2},\ \text{Pd-BaSO}_4} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2N-NH_2}} \mathrm{C}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CN} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{2.\ H_2O}]{\text{1.(DIBAL-H)}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\text{Dil. NaOH}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Thionyl chloride converts the acid to its acyl chloride; Rosenmund's reduction over palladium poisoned with barium sulphate then stops at the aldehyde; and hydrazine condenses with that aldehyde to give the hydrazone.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3COCl}\), ethanoyl chloride
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}N-NH_2}\), ethanal hydrazone

(b) Di-isobutylaluminium hydride reduces the nitrile only as far as the aldehyde, hydrolysis releasing it; dilute alkali then brings about an aldol addition between two molecules of that aldehyde; and heating dehydrates the aldol.
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO}\), 3-hydroxybutanal
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCHO}\), but-2-enal

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Glycosidic linkage
(b) Invert sugar
(c) Oligosaccharides
rows.solution:
(a) A glycosidic linkage is the oxygen bridge joining two monosaccharide units, formed when their hydroxyl groups condense with loss of water. It is the linkage that builds disaccharides and polysaccharides.

(b) Invert sugar is the equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose obtained by hydrolysing sucrose. The name records a change of sign: sucrose is dextrorotatory, but the fructose released is so strongly laevorotatory that the mixture's net rotation is to the left — the rotation has been inverted.

(c) Oligosaccharides are carbohydrates that yield between two and ten monosaccharide units on hydrolysis. Disaccharides such as sucrose, maltose and lactose are the commonest members.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Define reverse osmosis. Name one SPM which can be used in the process of reverse osmosis.
rows.context: The spontaneous flow of the solvent through a semipermeable membrane from a pure solvent to a solution or from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution is called osmosis. The phenomenon of osmosis can be demonstrated by taking two eggs of the same size. In an egg, the membrane below the shell and around the egg material is semipermeable. The outer hard shell can be removed by putting the egg in dilute hydrochloric acid. After removing the hard shell, one egg is placed in distilled water and the other in a saturated salt solution. After some time, the egg placed in distilled water swells-up while the egg placed in salt solution shrinks. The external pressure applied to stop the osmosis is termed as osmotic pressure (a colligative property). Reverse osmosis takes place when the applied external pressure becomes larger than the osmotic pressure.
rows.solution:
Reverse osmosis is the process in which a pressure GREATER than the osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side of a semi-permeable membrane, so that the solvent is driven backwards — from the solution to the pure solvent side — instead of flowing in the direction ordinary osmosis would take it.

A semi-permeable membrane used for it is cellulose acetate, which passes water but not the ions of dissolved salt. This is the basis of desalinating sea water.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: What do you expect to happen when red blood corpuscles (RBC's) are placed in 0.5% \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) solution ?
rows.context: The spontaneous flow of the solvent through a semipermeable membrane from a pure solvent to a solution or from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution is called osmosis. The phenomenon of osmosis can be demonstrated by taking two eggs of the same size. In an egg, the membrane below the shell and around the egg material is semipermeable. The outer hard shell can be removed by putting the egg in dilute hydrochloric acid. After removing the hard shell, one egg is placed in distilled water and the other in a saturated salt solution. After some time, the egg placed in distilled water swells-up while the egg placed in salt solution shrinks. The external pressure applied to stop the osmosis is termed as osmotic pressure (a colligative property). Reverse osmosis takes place when the applied external pressure becomes larger than the osmotic pressure.
rows.solution: Human red blood cells have an internal concentration equivalent to about 0.9% sodium chloride, so a 0.5% solution is HYPOTONIC — more dilute than the cell contents. Water therefore flows INTO the cells by osmosis. The cells swell, and if enough water enters they burst, a process called haemolysis. This endosmosis is why intravenous fluids must be isotonic with blood.

rows.stem: Which one of the following will have higher osmotic pressure in 1 M \(\mathrm{KCl}\) or 1 M urea solution. Justify your answer.
rows.context: The spontaneous flow of the solvent through a semipermeable membrane from a pure solvent to a solution or from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution is called osmosis. The phenomenon of osmosis can be demonstrated by taking two eggs of the same size. In an egg, the membrane below the shell and around the egg material is semipermeable. The outer hard shell can be removed by putting the egg in dilute hydrochloric acid. After removing the hard shell, one egg is placed in distilled water and the other in a saturated salt solution. After some time, the egg placed in distilled water swells-up while the egg placed in salt solution shrinks. The external pressure applied to stop the osmosis is termed as osmotic pressure (a colligative property). Reverse osmosis takes place when the applied external pressure becomes larger than the osmotic pressure.
rows.solution:
The 1 M potassium chloride solution has the higher osmotic pressure.

Osmotic pressure is a colligative property, \(\Pi = i\,C\,RT\), so it depends on the number of PARTICLES in solution. Urea is a non-electrolyte and does not dissociate, so \(i = 1\) and a 1 M solution gives 1 mol of particles per litre. Potassium chloride dissociates completely into \(\mathrm{K^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), so \(i = 2\) and the same 1 M concentration gives 2 mol of particles per litre — and therefore about twice the osmotic pressure.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Why osmotic pressure is a colligative property ?
rows.context: The spontaneous flow of the solvent through a semipermeable membrane from a pure solvent to a solution or from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution is called osmosis. The phenomenon of osmosis can be demonstrated by taking two eggs of the same size. In an egg, the membrane below the shell and around the egg material is semipermeable. The outer hard shell can be removed by putting the egg in dilute hydrochloric acid. After removing the hard shell, one egg is placed in distilled water and the other in a saturated salt solution. After some time, the egg placed in distilled water swells-up while the egg placed in salt solution shrinks. The external pressure applied to stop the osmosis is termed as osmotic pressure (a colligative property). Reverse osmosis takes place when the applied external pressure becomes larger than the osmotic pressure.
rows.solution: Because it depends only on the NUMBER of solute particles in the solution and not on their nature. A colligative property is by definition one determined by how many particles are present, and osmotic pressure obeys \(\Pi = CRT\), in which the concentration enters as moles of particles per unit volume and the identity of the solute appears nowhere. Two solutions of equal particle concentration exert equal osmotic pressures whatever the solutes are, which is what makes the property colligative.

rows.stem: Arrange the following in the increasing order of their basic character. Give reason :
rows.context: Amines have a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as Lewis base. Greater the value of \(\mathrm{K_b}\) or smaller the value of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), stronger is the base. Amines are more basic than alcohols, ethers, esters, etc. The basic character of aliphatic amines should increase with the increase of alkyl substitution. But it does not occur in a regular manner as a secondary aliphatic amine is unexpectedly more basic than a tertiary amine in aqueous solutions. Aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia and aliphatic amines. Electron releasing groups such as \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), etc., increase the basicity while electron-withdrawing substituents such as \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\), \(\mathrm{-CN}\), halogens etc., decrease the basicity of amines. The effect of these substitute is more at \(\mathrm{p}^{-}\) than at \(\mathrm{m}^{-}\) position.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED - 'the following' exists ONLY as three drawn benzene rings printed side by side and separated by commas: (1) a ring with NH2 at the top vertex (aniline); (2) a ring with NH2 at the top and NO2 at the para vertex (4-nitroaniline); (3) a ring with NO2 at the top and CH3 at the para vertex (4-nitrotoluene). The stem names no compound in text. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
[CBSE VOIDED this question. Its marking scheme prints the ranking and then adds: "Award full marks if attempted because of printing error." The error is in the third structure: as printed it is 4-nitrotoluene, which carries no amino group at all and so cannot be ranked for basic character alongside the other two. 4-Methylaniline, with \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) at the top and \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) at the para position, is evidently what was meant. The ranking below is the one the scheme gives, using the structures AS PRINTED.]

The three printed compounds are aniline, 4-nitroaniline and 4-nitrotoluene, and the scheme's increasing order of basic character is
4-nitrotoluene \(<\) 4-nitroaniline \(<\) aniline

The reasoning for the two that CAN be compared: in aniline the nitrogen lone pair is already delocalised into the ring, which weakens it as a base; adding a nitro group at the para position withdraws electron density both inductively and by resonance, pulling that lone pair still further away, so 4-nitroaniline is much the weaker base of the two. 4-Nitrotoluene has no basic nitrogen at all and is placed lowest on that ground.

Had the intended compound been 4-methylaniline, the order would run 4-nitroaniline \(<\) aniline \(<\) 4-methylaniline, the methyl group releasing electron density towards the ring and making the lone pair more available.

rows.stem: Why \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) of aniline is more than that of methylamine ?
rows.context: Amines have a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as Lewis base. Greater the value of \(\mathrm{K_b}\) or smaller the value of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), stronger is the base. Amines are more basic than alcohols, ethers, esters, etc. The basic character of aliphatic amines should increase with the increase of alkyl substitution. But it does not occur in a regular manner as a secondary aliphatic amine is unexpectedly more basic than a tertiary amine in aqueous solutions. Aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia and aliphatic amines. Electron releasing groups such as \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), etc., increase the basicity while electron-withdrawing substituents such as \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\), \(\mathrm{-CN}\), halogens etc., decrease the basicity of amines. The effect of these substitute is more at \(\mathrm{p}^{-}\) than at \(\mathrm{m}^{-}\) position.
rows.solution:
Because in aniline the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is much less available to accept a proton. The nitrogen is attached directly to an \(sp^2\) carbon of an aromatic system, and its lone pair takes part in the ring's \(\pi\) system; protonating it would destroy that stabilisation, which costs energy.

In methylamine no such delocalisation exists. Its lone pair sits on nitrogen, and the methyl group even pushes electron density towards it by the inductive effect, making it more available still. Methylamine is therefore the stronger base, and since a stronger base has the SMALLER \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), aniline's \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) is the larger.

rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the increasing order of their basic character in an aqueous solution :
\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N},\ \mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH},\ \mathrm{NH_3},\ \mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\)
rows.context: Amines have a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as Lewis base. Greater the value of \(\mathrm{K_b}\) or smaller the value of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), stronger is the base. Amines are more basic than alcohols, ethers, esters, etc. The basic character of aliphatic amines should increase with the increase of alkyl substitution. But it does not occur in a regular manner as a secondary aliphatic amine is unexpectedly more basic than a tertiary amine in aqueous solutions. Aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia and aliphatic amines. Electron releasing groups such as \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), etc., increase the basicity while electron-withdrawing substituents such as \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\), \(\mathrm{-CN}\), halogens etc., decrease the basicity of amines. The effect of these substitute is more at \(\mathrm{p}^{-}\) than at \(\mathrm{m}^{-}\) position.
rows.solution:
Three effects act at once in aqueous solution and they do not all point the same way. The inductive effect of the methyl groups raises basicity as more of them are added. Steric crowding lowers it, since bulky groups hinder a proton's approach. And solvation lowers it too: the more hydrogens the cation has on nitrogen, the more hydrogen bonds it can make to water, so \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_3^+}\) with three is far better stabilised than \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{NH^+}\) with one.

For methyl groups the balance gives
\(\mathrm{NH_3} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N} < \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH}\)
Note that ammonia is the weakest of the four, having no alkyl group at all, and that the tertiary amine sits SECOND rather than last — the order is not monotonic in the number of methyl groups, which is the whole point.

rows.stem: Why ammonolysis of alkyl halides is not a good method to prepare pure amines ?
rows.context: Amines have a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen atom due to which they behave as Lewis base. Greater the value of \(\mathrm{K_b}\) or smaller the value of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), stronger is the base. Amines are more basic than alcohols, ethers, esters, etc. The basic character of aliphatic amines should increase with the increase of alkyl substitution. But it does not occur in a regular manner as a secondary aliphatic amine is unexpectedly more basic than a tertiary amine in aqueous solutions. Aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia and aliphatic amines. Electron releasing groups such as \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), etc., increase the basicity while electron-withdrawing substituents such as \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\), \(\mathrm{-CN}\), halogens etc., decrease the basicity of amines. The effect of these substitute is more at \(\mathrm{p}^{-}\) than at \(\mathrm{m}^{-}\) position.
rows.solution:
Because the reaction cannot be stopped at one substitution. The primary amine formed in the first step is itself a nucleophile, and at least as good a one as ammonia, so it attacks a further molecule of the alkyl halide to give a secondary amine; that in turn gives a tertiary amine, and that a quaternary ammonium salt.
\(\mathrm{RX} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NH_3}} \mathrm{RNH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{RX}} \mathrm{R_2NH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{RX}} \mathrm{R_3N} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{RX}} \mathrm{R_4N^+X^-}\)
The product is therefore a MIXTURE of all four, difficult and wasteful to separate. Using a large excess of ammonia favours the primary amine but does not give it pure.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(a) Give IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CHO}\).
(b) Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between propanal and propanone.
(c) How will you convert the following :
(i) Toluene to benzoic acid
(ii) Ethanol to propan-2-ol
(iii) Propanal to 2-hydroxy propanoic acid
rows.solution:
(a) The chain is four carbons with an aldehyde at one end, numbered from that end, and the double bond starts at C-2:
but-2-enal

(b) Use the iodoform test. Propanone is a methyl ketone, so warming it with sodium hydroxide and iodine gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; propanal has an ethyl group next to its carbonyl and gives none. Tollens' reagent would serve equally well the other way round — propanal reduces it and propanone does not.

(c)(i) Toluene to benzoic acid. Hot alkaline potassium permanganate oxidises the whole side chain to a single carboxyl carbon, and acidification liberates the acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KMnO_4}\text{-}\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOK} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

(ii) Ethanol to propan-2-ol. Oxidise the alcohol to the aldehyde with PCC, then add a methyl Grignard and hydrolyse; the new methyl group makes the three-carbon secondary alcohol.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCC}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow[\text{2. }\mathrm{H_3O^+}]{\text{1. }\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}\)

(iii) Propanal to 2-hydroxypropanoic acid. Oxidise to the acid, halogenate at the \(\alpha\) position by the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction, then hydrolyse the halide.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{CH_3CHClCOOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)COOH}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Complete each synthesis by giving missing starting material, reagent or products :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — REQUIRED - all five sub-parts (a) to (e) are drawn structural schemes and nothing else; the stem alone contains no chemistry at all. (a) cyclopentanone + HO-NH2, over an arrow labelled H+; (b) a question mark, over an arrow labelled (i) O3 / (ii) Zn - H2O, giving '2' of a six-membered ring drawn as =O; (c) a cyclohexane ring bearing two COOH groups on adjacent carbons, over an arrow labelled SOCl2 above and a heat symbol below; (d) a cyclohexane ring bearing CHO and COOH on adjacent carbons, over an arrow labelled NaCN/HCl; (e) a benzene ring, an unlabelled arrow, and a benzene ring bearing C(=O)CH3 (acetophenone). Sub-parts (a) and (b) are on page idx 18; (c), (d) and (e) at the top of page idx 20.
rows.solution:
All five sub-parts are printed as drawn reaction schemes with no words, so each is named here before it is answered.

(a) Cyclopentanone is treated with hydroxylamine in the presence of acid. The carbonyl condenses with the reagent and water is eliminated, giving the oxime:
cyclopentanone oxime, the five-membered ring carrying \(\mathrm{{=}N-OH}\) in place of \(\mathrm{{=}O}\).

(b) The missing starting material is asked for: ozonolysis followed by reductive work-up with zinc and water gives TWO molecules of cyclohexanone. Ozonolysis cleaves a carbon-carbon double bond and puts an oxygen on each of the carbons that carried it, so running that backwards, the substrate must be the alkene formed by joining two cyclohexanone carbonyl carbons:
cyclohexylidenecyclohexane, two cyclohexane rings joined by a \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond.

(c) Benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid (phthalic acid) is treated with thionyl chloride and heated. Thionyl chloride converts a carboxyl group to an acyl chloride, and here it converts both:
benzene-1,2-dicarbonyl dichloride (phthaloyl chloride), the ring carrying two \(-\mathrm{COCl}\) groups on adjacent carbons.

(d) 2-Formylbenzoic acid is treated with sodium cyanide and hydrochloric acid. Cyanide adds across the ALDEHYDE group only — a carboxyl group does not undergo nucleophilic addition — giving the cyanohydrin:
2-[cyano(hydroxy)methyl]benzoic acid, the ring carrying \(-\mathrm{CH(OH)CN}\) and \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) on adjacent carbons.

(e) The missing reagent is asked for: benzene is converted to acetophenone. That is a Friedel-Crafts acylation, so the reagent is an acylating agent with a Lewis acid catalyst:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCl}\) with anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\), or equally \((\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}\) with anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\).

rows.stem:
(a) Calculate the standard Gibbs energy \((\Delta_\mathrm{r}\mathrm{G}^{\circ})\) of the following reaction at 25 °C :
\(\mathrm{Au(s)} + \mathrm{Ca^{2+}(1M)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Au^{3+}(1M)} + \mathrm{Ca(s)}\)
\(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Au^{3+}/Au}} = +\,1.5\) V, \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ca^{2+}/Ca}} = -\,2.87\) V
Predict whether the reaction will be spontaneous or not at 25 °C.
[1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
(b) Tarnished silver contains \(\mathrm{Ag_2S}\). Can this tarnish be removed by placing tarnished silverware in an aluminium pan containing an inert electrolytic solution such as \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) ? The standard electrode potential for half reaction :
\(\mathrm{Ag_2S(s)} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Ag(s)} + \mathrm{S^{2-}}\) is \(-0.71\) V and for
\(\mathrm{Al^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Al(s)}\) is \(-1.66\) V
rows.solution:
(a) [The printed equation, \(\mathrm{Au} + \mathrm{Ca^{2+}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Au^{3+}} + \mathrm{Ca}\), is not balanced in electrons; \(2\mathrm{Au} + 3\mathrm{Ca^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Au^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Ca}\) is, and that balancing is what fixes \(n\). CBSE did not void this question, and its scheme takes \(n = 6\), which is the balanced value.]

Gold is oxidised, so it is the anode, and calcium is reduced at the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = (-2.87) - (+1.5) = -4.37\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing electrons gives six transferred, so \(n = 6\):
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} = -(6 \times 96500 \times (-4.37)) = +2530230\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
that is \(+2530.23\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

The free energy change is POSITIVE, so the reaction is NON-SPONTANEOUS at 25 °C. That is chemically what one would expect: gold is the least reactive metal here and calcium among the most, so gold displacing calcium runs the reactivity series backwards.

(b) [The aluminium half-reaction is printed as \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}} + 3e^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Al(s)}\), with a stray coefficient 2; three electrons reduce ONE aluminium ion. The potential quoted is unaffected.]

Yes, the tarnish can be removed.

Aluminium has the more negative standard electrode potential of the two, \(-1.66\) V against \(-0.71\) V, so aluminium is the stronger reducing agent. Placing the tarnished silver in contact with aluminium in an electrolyte lets aluminium reduce the silver in \(\mathrm{Ag_2S}\) back to metallic silver, dissolving itself as \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) instead. Taking the cell made of the two half reactions,
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = (-0.71) - (-1.66) = +0.95\ \mathrm{V}\)

A positive cell potential means a negative free energy change, so the reaction is feasible and the tarnish is removed. Note that the silver is RECOVERED rather than polished away, which is why this method is preferred to abrasive cleaning.

rows.stem:
(a) Define the following :
(i) Cell potential
(ii) Fuel cell
(b) Calculate emf of the following cell at 25 °C :
\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}_{(0.1M)}} \parallel \mathrm{Cd^{2+}_{(0.01M)}} \mid \mathrm{Cd(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cd^{2+}/Cd}} = -0.40\) V
\(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = -0.76\) V
\([\log 10 = 1]\)
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Cell potential is the difference in electrode potential between the two electrodes of a galvanic cell — the potential of the cathode minus that of the anode. When both half-cells are in their standard states it is called the standard cell potential, \(E^{\circ}_{cell}\), and it is the electrical driving force of the cell reaction.

(ii) A fuel cell is a galvanic cell in which the energy of combustion of a fuel is converted DIRECTLY into electrical energy, without first being turned into heat. Its reactants are supplied continuously from outside rather than stored inside, so it runs as long as fuel is fed; the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is the standard example.

(b) Zinc is written on the left, so it is the anode; cadmium is the cathode.
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cd^{2+}/Cd}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = (-0.40) - (-0.76) = 0.36\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cd^{2+}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cd(s)}\), so \(n = 2\):
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cd^{2+}}]}\)
\(= 0.36 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.1}{0.01} = 0.36 - 0.0295\log 10\)
\(= 0.36 - 0.0295 = 0.3305\ \mathrm{V}\)

rows.stem: An organic compound 'A', molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\) oxidises with \(\mathrm{CrO_3}\) to form a compound 'B'. Compound 'B' on warming with iodine and aqueous solution of NaOH gives a yellow precipitate of compound 'C'. When compound 'A' is heated with conc. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at 413 K gives a compound 'D', which on reaction with excess HI gives compound 'E'. Identify compounds 'A', 'B', 'C', 'D' and 'E' and write chemical equations involved.
rows.solution:
The formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_6O}\) with these reactions identifies 'A' as ethanol, and everything follows.

Chromium trioxide oxidises the primary alcohol to the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)
so \(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal.

Iodine with aqueous sodium hydroxide is the iodoform test, and ethanal answers it because it has a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group; the yellow precipitate is iodoform:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CHI_3} + \mathrm{HCOONa} + 3\mathrm{NaI} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
so \(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CHI_3}\), iodoform.

Concentrated sulphuric acid at 413 K is the LOWER of the two dehydration temperatures and gives the ether rather than the alkene:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
so \(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3}\), ethoxyethane. At 443 K it would have given ethene instead, which is why the temperature is specified.

Excess hydroiodic acid cleaves the ether at both \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bonds:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3} + 2\mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CH_3CH_2I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
so \(\mathrm{E} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2I}\), iodoethane.

rows.stem:
(a) Write chemical equations of the following reactions :
(i) Phenol is treated with conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
(ii) Propene is treated with \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) followed by oxidation by \(\mathrm{H_2O_2/OH^{-}}\).
(iii) Sodium t-butoxide is treated with \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\).
(b) Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.
(c) Arrange the following in increasing order of acid strength :
phenol, ethanol, water
rows.solution:
(a)(i) Concentrated nitric acid nitrates all three activated positions of phenol at once, giving picric acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{2,4,6\text{-}(O_2N)_3{-}C_6H_2{-}OH}\)

(ii) Hydroboration-oxidation adds water across the double bond with ANTI-Markovnikov orientation, so the hydroxyl group ends up on the terminal carbon:
\(3\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2} + (\mathrm{BH_3})_2 \longrightarrow 2(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2})_3\mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{3\mathrm{H_2O_2},\ \mathrm{OH^-}} 6\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\)
The product is propan-1-ol, not propan-2-ol.

(iii) This is Williamson ether synthesis. The alkoxide attacks the carbon bearing the halogen, and the choice of partners matters: the bulky tert-butoxide is the ALKOXIDE and the unhindered methyl chloride the halide, so substitution succeeds.
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-ONa} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O-CH_3} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)
The product is 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane. Reversing the roles — sodium methoxide with a tert-butyl halide — would eliminate instead and give 2-methylpropene.

(b) Use the iodoform test. Butan-2-ol has the \(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)-}\) grouping, so warming it with sodium hydroxide and iodine gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform; butan-1-ol, whose hydroxyl is on a terminal carbon, gives none. The Lucas test would also separate them, but more slowly: secondary in about five minutes, primary not at all at room temperature.

(c) Acidity is decided by how stable the anion left behind is. The ethoxide ion is destabilised by the electron-releasing ethyl group, so ethanol is the weakest acid — weaker even than water, whose hydroxide carries no such group. The phenoxide ion has its negative charge delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance and is much the best stabilised, so phenol is the strongest. The increasing order is
ethanol \(<\) water \(<\) phenol
